When to avoid:

1.  Avoid overloading buttons on one page or proximity of two or more buttons to each other, which may create visual overload and difficulty in making decisions.

2. When you wish to direct the user to additional information, you must use the link and avoid using the button.

Recommendations for buttons from the government language characterization guide:

It is recommended to read the dedicated instructions for the buttons in the government language characterization guide -

Guidelines for writing according to situations (harhayeda.gov.il)

Do and Don't
Do
The action of the button must be explained by the text placed on the button. You can add a icon on the button to add relevant information. In addition, you must use up to 1-3 words (2-15 characters) on the button.
Don’t
Don't use two lines of text on a button.
Do
When using multiple buttons, designate the more important action as a primary button and the less important action as a secondary button or text button.
Don’t
Don't use two main buttons side by side.
Do
Use one primary button and let the other buttons be all secondary.
Don’t
Don't use several types of buttons for a section such as primary, secondary and text.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Contrast Ratio: Ensure the button has sufficient color contrast. The contrast ratio must be at least 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text. You can find the guidelines for color contrast in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum). 

Keyboard Navigation: The button must be fully accessible via keyboard. Ensure that the button can receive focus using the Tab key and can be activated with the Enter or Space keys. This complies with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard. 

Focus Indicators: When the button is focused, there must be a visible focus indicator to help users with keyboard navigation. This is required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible. 

Accessible Name: For icon-only buttons, always provide an aria-label that clearly describes the button's function. This adheres to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value. 

Avoid Redundant ARIA Attributes: When using semantic elements like <button>, avoid using redundant ARIA attributes like role="button" or tabindex, which are already inherently included. This follows best practices outlined in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.1: Parsing.

design.title: Design
design.content:
Progress timed button




Anatomy:

Lable - The text on the button that links the action to the user

Timer - Countdown to the start or end of an action

Icon - Accompany the text and timer with a button

Container - The area that contains the label and countdown and defines the size and shape of the button

Linear background (optional) - Visually describes to the user when time is up

States:
On Progress Button's states:

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When users need to take a moment to consider their decision before taking irreversible actions, such as deleting important data

To allow users a short window to cancel or confirm an automated process, such as submitting a form or initiating an action

When it is important to clearly communicate the time remaining for an action, ensuring that users are informed and can act accordingly

When to avoid:

For standard actions without a time limit, a regular button would be more appropriate

When users need significant time to review or gather information before acting, a timed button may add unnecessary pressure

Users with disabilities may have difficulty interacting with a timer due to inadequate alternatives or support

For repetitive or quick actions, the added timer may serve the user flow

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Adjust the delay duration to the context - not too short or too long.
Don’t
Do not use visual display only without the timer
Do
Use short and clear titles.
Don’t
Do not use 2 lines.
Examples

The action is given as long as the time does not run out.

When the time is up - the button will be clickable

When time is up - we'll move to another place.

When to use:

To highlight the most important action on a screen.

When a single primary action needs to be easily accessible.

In applications where space is limited, but key action needs to stand out.

To provide quick access to frequently used features, such as adding a new item or writing a message.

When to avoid:

When several primary actions must be presented equally.

In contexts where a floating button may obscure important content.

On screens where the main action is already clearly marked and easily accessible through other user interface elements.

In situations where the use of a floating button may cause confusion or disrupt the user flow.

Hierarchy and location

Several types of buttons can be used to express different levels of emphasis.

Which gives us sets of roles of do's and don'ts when it comes to putting them together.

In a bottom bar, when using multiple buttons, indicate the more important action by placing it in an included button next to a text button or secondary button.

Never use two primary buttons next to each other, as this will confuse the user with the hierarchy.

The exception to this role is using a primary button with a floating button:

This screen layout uses: 

1. Expanded floating action button for highest emphasis 

2. Button contains for high emphasis

3. Text button for low emphasis

When the FAB button is used as an action that is not the most important such as: Back to top, We will use it in Secondary mode

Do
Sometimes there will be cases where we use 2 FAB one above the other such as: a btt button and a chat button
Don’t
Don't use several floating buttons on one page
Do
The button will get its color from the palette colors of the interface.
Don’t
Don't add a badge to a FAB
Do
Use a clear action icon on the FAB.
Don’t

Do
Unlike the standard floating button - in the extended mode you can use a label without an icon.
Don’t
Don't use the floating button in its expanded state with only an icon.
Do
A floating button affects the entire page and not specific elements on the page.

Don't - Individual components such as cards cannot have a floating button per card.

Split Button.name: Split Button

design.title: Design
design.content:
Split Button
Split Button Open
Split Button

Anatomy

Main Button - Triggers the default and most common action on click (e.g. "Save").

Dropdown Button - An icon button that opens a menu containing related or alternative actions.

Dropdown Menu - A list of secondary actions that offer variations or extensions to the main action.

Menu Item - Action to select within the drop-down menu.




Types




Direction

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When there is a primary action that users are likely to perform frequently, but it is also necessary to offer related actions.

When a repetitive workflow can be streamlined and the most frequently used action can be quickly accessed.

When several similar actions need to be grouped under one control (for example: different file formats, different save types).

When to avoid:

When there is no clear action – if all options are equally important, it is better to use a regular menu or Dropdown.

When the actions are not related to each other – such grouping can confuse users.

When the target audience includes users with low digital literacy – a split button may be less understandable.

When the component is placed in crowded areas of the interface, which are difficult to click precisely – especially on mobile, unless the component is optimized for this.

When users are expected to frequently use several actions – it is better to present the actions in a visible and accessible way.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Consistency must be maintained between the Main Button and the Dropdown Button.
Don’t
Do not design the dropdown button differently from the main button.
Do
Consistency must be maintained between the Main Button and the Dropdown Button.
Don’t
Do not design the dropdown button differently from the main button.
Do
The icon should be placed to the right of the text in the main button.
Don’t
Do not place an icon to the left of the text in the main button and vice versa when the direction is LTR.
Do
Uniformity must be maintained in the presentation of options.
Don’t
Do not combine options with and without icons in the same menu.
Examples and uses
Do
The main operation is located on the main button for quick and convenient execution
Do
Pressing the main button performs the action.
Do
Clicking on the dropdown displays additional actions.
Do
Selecting from the list performs the action immediately.
Do
When the default action is updated, the previous action will appear in the drop-down list of options.
Do
Selecting the same action again will set it as the default on the main button

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

Can be used in forms, in models or on side panels.

Used to filter data on a page, menu or within a component. Check boxes are in the data table for batch editing purposes.

Check Terms - Turning the input on or off The checkbox can indicate whether you agree to the terms.

Lists with sub-choices

When to avoid:

Don't use a component if users can only select one option from a selection. In this case, use the radio component.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Use a checkbox to mark conditions
Don’t
Don't use checkboxes when only one item can be selected. In that case use a radio button.
Do
Use as multiple selection filtering
Do
Place the text and the checkbox on the same line so that the control and the label are aligned at the top.
Don’t
Don't vertically center wrapped text with the checkbox.
Do
Use the Neutral marker – only when some of the options are checked
Do
Use a tab when there is a choice from several options from the same category (for example, selecting a gender)
Don’t
Do not use the neutral marker if it is not the parent influencing the other markings







Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: 

Ensure checkboxes are focusable via the Tab key and can be toggled on/off using Space or Enter. This makes checkboxes fully operable for keyboard-only users, aligning with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard. 

Checkbox Groups: If multiple checkboxes are grouped (such as in a list of preferences), ensure proper navigation using Tab between checkboxes, and Space or Enter to toggle each one. This supports efficient navigation within a group, as recommended by WAI-ARIA Checkbox Design Patterns. 

Screen Reader Support: 

Role and State: Use role="checkbox" and aria-checked attributes to indicate whether the checkbox is checked (true), unchecked (false), or indeterminate (mixed). This allows screen readers to announce the state of the checkbox accurately, ensuring compliance with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value. 

Indeterminate State: For checkboxes that support a mixed state (partially checked), use aria-checked="mixed" to announce the checkbox as being in an indeterminate state. This state is commonly used for parent checkboxes when some but not all child options are selected, as described in WAI-ARIA Checkbox Mixed State  

Focus Indicators: 

Checkboxes must have a visible focus indicator when they receive keyboard focus. This ensures that keyboard-only users can track which element is currently active, in line with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible. 

Make sure the focus indicator is clear, particularly when navigating through a list of checkboxes, so that users can easily see where they are within the form. 

Contrast and Visibility: 

The checkbox itself (including the checkmark, indeterminate mark, and background) must meet the required contrast ratio of at least 3:1 for graphical elements, according to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast. 

Ensure that checked, unchecked, and indeterminate states are visually distinct from each other to make the component accessible for users with visual impairments. 

Error Identification and Handling: 

When validation is required (e.g., ensuring at least one checkbox is selected), clearly indicate any errors. Use aria-invalid="true" and link error messages using aria-errormessage to improve accessibility for screen reader users, as per WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification. 

Error Suggestion: If a user attempts to submit a form without selecting the required checkboxes, provide clear error suggestions (e.g., "Please select at least one option"). This follows the recommendations from WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3: Error Suggestion. 

Form Integration: 

Name and Value for Form Submission: Each checkbox should have a unique value and share the same name attribute if they belong to the same group. This ensures that multiple selections can be submitted as part of form data, adhering to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.3: Status Messages. 

Required Checkboxes: If a checkbox is required, make it clear to the user by using aria-required="true" and visually indicating the requirement (e.g., with an asterisk). This complies with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.5: Identify Input Purpose. 

Help and Guidance Text: 

Provide help or guidance text using aria-describedby to link additional information to the checkbox or checkbox group. This is particularly useful when explaining what selections mean or if a checkbox is indeterminate. This improves usability for screen reader users, in line with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships.

Check box.summary: Used when there are multiple items to select in a list. Users can select zero, one, or any number of items.

Toggle (Switch).name: Toggle (Switch)

design.title: Design
design.content:
To display designs, use an upload section:

Anatomy

To display designs, use an upload section:

Track- The background of the component, which indicates whether it is on or off

Thumb- The button that moves on the Track between the modes

Label- Description of the action that is activated using the Toggle




States

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to Use:

To toggle between binary settings, such as on/off, enable/disable, or show/hide.

When to Avoid:

When it is a non-binary option. In such a case the checkbox should be used.

Highlights-

It is required to decide what the default state is

When the action has a significant consequence, the accidental activation of which could lead to damage, an additional indication must be added to confirm the action - for example using a tooltip

Do and Don't
Do
Put the text on the right with the reading direction, so that it is clear what is lit.
Don’t
Don't Put the text of the toggle to the left of the text
Example

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: 

Toggle switches must be fully operable using the keyboard. Users should be able to focus on the toggle using the Tab key and toggle its state using Space or Enter keys. 

The state (on/off) should be announced to screen readers through aria-checked attribute. 

Ensure the toggle is focusable and navigable, following WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard. 

Screen Reader Support: 

Use the role="switch" and aria-checked attributes to indicate the toggle's on/off state. This tells screen readers whether the switch is activated or not, ensuring compliance with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value. 

Provide accessible labels for the toggle using aria-label or visually associated <label> elements, as described in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships. 

Focus Indicators: 

When the toggle is focused, there should be a visible focus indicator to make it clear to the user which element is active. This is a requirement in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible. 

Ensure focus order is logical and intuitive, guiding users through form controls in a predictable manner. 

Contrast and Visibility: 

Ensure the toggle is visually distinct from the background and its surrounding elements, particularly in its active, inactive, and focus states. A contrast ratio of at least 3:1 is required for graphical objects (e.g., icons used in the toggle switch) per WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast. 

Error Identification and Handling: 

When a toggle is required or involved in form validation, clearly communicate errors to the user by using aria-invalid="true" or aria-errormessage to link an error message element. This improves accessibility per WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3: Error Suggestion. 

Form Integration: 

The toggle must be able to be programmatically associated with a form for submission using the name and value attributes. When used in forms, the state (on/off) should be reflected in form data submission in compliance with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.3: Status Messages. 

Required Fields: 

If the toggle switch is required, use the aria-required="true" attribute to indicate to assistive technologies that the toggle must be selected to pass form validation. This follows WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.5: Identify Input Purpose.

Toggle (Switch).summary: The component allows you to turn a certain action on or off, or switch between modes.

Slider.name: Slider

design.title: Design
design.content:
Anatomy

Parameter Icon- An icon located to the left of the Slider and representing the parameter being controlled

Slider Line- A horizontal line that acts as a scale for values, ranging from 0% (minimum) to 100% (maximum). The track changes color from light to dark as the value increases.

Slider knob- The draggable element that represents the selected value

Value Indicator- Indicates the current value selected by the user.

Title- A short description explaining the adjusted parameter

Progress
States

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When a value within a specified range is required

When you want to provide an intuitive and quick way to adjust settings

When to Avoid:

When multiple values ​​need to be selected

When values ​​outside a specified range need to be selected

When precise values ​​need to be entered using a keyboard

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Ensure clear spacing between sliders for clarity.
Don’t
This element should not be used when a choice needs to be made between two single values.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility
Keyboard Navigation 

Users must be able to interact with the range component using only a keyboard: 

Tab moves focus between the range handles. 

Left and Right arrows decrease/increase the value by step. 

Home moves the slider to the minimum value. 

End moves the slider to the maximum value. 

 

Screen Reader Support 

The component must provide appropriate ARIA attributes: 

role="slider" for single and dual-handle sliders. 

aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, and aria-valuenow must reflect the current slider values. 

For dual sliders, both handles should have separate aria-valuetext attributes describing the min/max range. 

Labels should be linked using aria-labelledby. 

 

Guidelines 

Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard – The range must be fully operable via keyboard. 

Success Criterion 2.4.3: Focus Order – Logical focus navigation. 

Success Criterion 2.5.1: Pointer Gestures – Ensures the slider works for different input devices. 

Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships – Labels and descriptions should be properly linked. 

Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value – The slider’s role and values must be correctly conveyed to assistive technologies. 

Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) – Ensures readability.

Anatomy

States

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to Use:

When a user has to choose one option from a list of 3 to 5 options.

When it is necessary to display all the options available for selection, and not hide them in a drop-down menu.

When to avoid:

When a user can select multiple options from a list. In this case Checkbox should be used.

For binary choices (yes/no), it is better to consider using Toggle for a more intuitive interface.

When the list of options is too long (more than 5) you should use the dropdown.

Do and Don'ts
Do
Use when there is only one choice.
Don’t
Don't-don't use for multiple choice. Use a checkbox instead
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: 

Radio Buttons: Each radio button must be navigable using the Tab key and selectable with Space or Enter. This allows keyboard-only users to cycle through the options and make selections without a mouse. This adheres to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard. 

Radio Group: When using a radio group, ensure that Arrow Up and Arrow Down keys allow users to move between options in the group, as recommended in WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices for Radio Group. This intuitive navigation allows users to efficiently choose between options in a grouped set. 

Screen Reader Support: 

Role and Labels: Each radio button should have the role="radio" attribute, and related radio buttons should be grouped using role="radiogroup". This provides the correct semantic meaning to screen readers and allows them to announce that the radio button is part of a group. Labels must be linked using either a visible <label> element or aria-label to provide context for each button, ensuring compliance with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value. 

State Announcement: Use the aria-checked attribute on each radio button to indicate its state (true for selected, false for unselected). This ensures screen readers announce the correct selection state, following the guidelines in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.3: Status Messages. 

Focus Indicators: 

Focus Management: Ensure a clear focus indicator when a radio button or group gains focus. This helps users with keyboard navigation understand which element is currently selected. Proper focus management is critical for accessibility and is required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible. 

Focus Order: When navigating between radio buttons, ensure the focus order is logical and follows the visual order, guiding users predictably through the form. 

Error Identification and Handling: 

Validation and Required Fields: If the radio group is part of a required selection in a form, errors should be identified clearly. Use aria-invalid="true" and aria-errormessage to link error messages to the radio group, ensuring that users receive feedback on why a selection is invalid. This is aligned with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3: Error Suggestion. 

Required Field: If a radio group is required, make it clear to users and assistive technology by using aria-required="true" or marking it visually with the required attribute in compliance with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.5: Identify Input Purpose. 

Contrast and Visibility: 

Ensure that each radio button, including the focus indicator and any surrounding text, meets the minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for text and 3:1 for graphical objects, as specified in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast. This ensures that the radio buttons are clearly visible to all users, including those with low vision or color blindness. 

Form Integration: 

Grouping Radio Buttons: Related radio buttons should be grouped using a fieldset and legend to provide a contextual 

Name and Value for Form Submission: Ensure each radio button has a unique value and that the name attribute is shared within the group, allowing form submissions to capture the selected option. This aligns with the form interaction guidelines in WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.3: Status Messages.

design.content:
Anatomy

Input box- The base of the component, where the user enters the requested input

Input text- The input text that the user enters

Label- Description of the requested input

Icon- Insert an icon that indicates the requested content, such as the NIS sign (optional)

Mandatory star- Marks a mandatory field (optional)

Tooltip Icon- The Icon that opens the Tooltip. Suitable for non-critical information that users may be looking for. It is required to create a Tooltip with the additional explanation (optional)

Question Tooltip- A prompting question that leads to opening a Tooltip. Suitable for critical information, which is not suitable to write in Help text. It is required to create a Tooltip with the additional explanation. (optional)

States

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When you need to enter unique information that cannot be predicted with a predetermined set of options.

When you need to enter memorable data that can be entered faster in freehand format versus more complex control.




When to avoid:

If you can only enter an option from a predefined list, avoid using free text entry as it may cause an error. Consider using a selection control such as a dropdown.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
The label should always be visible. If you decided to show it inside the container as soon as the user clicks, the label should move from the middle of the text field to the top (of the selected field).
Don’t
The label text should not be long or take up several lines.
Do
Replace help text with error text when needed
Don’t
Don't put error text below help text
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: 

The input component must be fully operable using the Tab key to navigate between form fields and Enter or Space for submission or interaction. This is essential for keyboard-only users and aligns with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard. 

Ensure that focus is properly managed, especially when an input field opens a dropdown or modal, so that the user can easily return to the form without losing context. 

Screen Reader Support: 

Inputs should always have associated labels. Use the <label> element or aria-label/aria-labelledby for screen readers to identify the input field. This complies with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value. 

Use aria-invalid to communicate input validity. For example, when a field has an invalid input, screen readers will announce that the field is incorrect, adhering to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification. 

If additional context or explanation is needed for an input (e.g., format or special requirements), use aria-describedby to link the input to supplementary text that explains more, ensuring alignment with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1. 

Focus Indicators: 

Input fields must have visible focus indicators when they are active. This is critical for users navigating via the keyboard, enabling them to see which field is in focus. This guideline follows WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible. 

If the focus changes dynamically (for example, in modal or autocomplete input fields), ensure that the focus management is logical and predictable. This improves the user experience for both keyboard and screen reader users. 

Error Identification and Feedback: 

Form validation errors must be clearly indicated. When an input fails validation, it should trigger both a visual error message and an auditory announcement via aria-errormessage linked to a descriptive element. This ensures that users, including those using screen readers, receive proper feedback, as required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3: Error Suggestion. 

If the input is required for form submission, it should be marked with aria-required="true" or the required attribute, and the user should be notified when this requirement is not met. 

Contrast and Visibility: 

Text inside the input field, including placeholder text, must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against the background for regular-sized text, as specified by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum). 

Ensure that the input border and any icons or decorations (e.g., validation icons or clear buttons) meet a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 for graphical elements, as required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast. 

Auto-completion and Input Suggestions: 

When offering input suggestions (e.g., autocomplete), ensure that the suggestions are easily navigable via the keyboard and that screen readers announce them appropriately. This can be managed by using aria-autocomplete and aria-expanded to signal when options are being displayed, in line with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1. 

Enable users to understand the input’s expected format by providing help text or examples using aria-describedby. 

Form Integration: 

Inputs must be associated with their parent forms using the form attribute or must be embedded directly within the form to ensure proper submission behavior, in line with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.3: Status Messages. 

Ensure the input’s name and value attributes are properly set to capture data during form submission. The name is particularly important to identify the input’s role within the form data. 

Required Fields and Guidance: 

If the input is a required field, it must be clearly communicated to the user, both visually and programmatically (e.g., aria-required="true"). For screen reader users, this ensures they understand which fields must be filled out, in accordance with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3: Error Suggestion. 

Offer guidance text for special input formats (e.g., date, phone number) by linking help text to the input via aria-describedby.

When to use:

To help the user navigate within the interface using search terms.

At the page level when searching for content on a specific page or at the component level when searching for data in a specific component, such as a data table.

It is best to place the element in the headers or navigation area for easy access.

When to avoid:

On sites where there is little content and you can navigate more precisely using the navigation bar.

It should be avoided as a substitute for a good navigation structure or clear content organization.

Avoid using if the search makes it difficult to locate the requested content.

Highlights

The location of the search is important - if the search is in the Header it will be linked to the search for the entire site, if the search is at the top of the page - it will be linked to the search only on that page, as is the case with a table and the like.




The icon that appears in the List Item will change according to the following situations (referring to the search results that open):

Clock Icon - when looking for something we've already looked for before

File Icon - when searching for a file

Government office Icon - when looking for a specific government office

Collapsed mode will be used on mobile (due to lack of space)

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Make sure the search field is clearly identifiable, with a magnifying glass icon to indicate its function.
Don’t
Avoid adding too many filters or advanced options directly in the search field. Keep the initial experience simple, with advanced options available when needed.
Do
Offer autocomplete or suggestions as users type to speed up the search process and help them find what they're looking for quickly.
Don’t
Avoid being too strict with spelling and formatting. Implement tolerance for typos or slight variations to improve the search experience.
Do
Provide a clear button ('X' icon) within the field to allow users to quickly reset their search query.
Don’t
Do not hide the search field under menus or other user interface elements. It should be easily accessible without requiring additional clicks or actions.
Do
We will use when dealing with very large datasets, dividing the search space can help improve efficiency and reduce the time required to find the information you want.
Don’t
We will not use when the two searches are not related to each other
Do

Don’t

Anatomy

Label- Tells the user what date to enter in the Date Field or Calendar Picker

Mandatory star- Mandatory field marking

Date field- A text box where the selected date is displayed and can also be entered manually

Calendar Icon- A calendar icon indicating that the calendar menu is available

Arrow navigation- Arrows for navigating between the months and years

Variants

Date field- We will use if the required date can be easily remembered by the user (credit validity for example) or if the required date is approximate (say only month and year).

Date Picker - We will use it when the user needs to choose an exact date and see it together with other dates (for example when making appointments or choosing a date of birth). The user can choose from the calendar or enter manually in the input field.

States

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When asking the user for an exact, approximate, or memorable date or time.

For scheduling tasks.

Highlights:

Clicking on the Calendar icon opens or closes the Calendar View (also closes by clicking outside of it)

By clicking on the Date Field you can enter the date manually.

On mobile, the priority is to use the Calendar Picker.

Do not change the length and width of the calendar according to the screen size. The component size must be maintained on all screens.

Even when there is a calendar for choosing a date, you must give the option to manually enter the date using the Field.

Do not require the user to enter special characters for the date format ("/", ".", "-")

Do's and Don'ts
Do
The width sizes of all screen types must be maintained
Don’t
Do not - do not expand the component
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation 

Navigating the Calendar: Users should be able to open the calendar using the Enter or Space key. Once the calendar is open, they should use Arrow keys (Left, Right, Up, Down) to navigate between days. Tab key should be used to navigate between controls (e.g., next month, previous month, today button, etc.). This follows WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard. 

Selecting Dates: A selected date can be confirmed by pressing the Enter or Space key. Users should also be able to use the Escape key to close the calendar dropdown without making a selection. 

Month and Year Navigation: Use keyboard shortcuts like Page Up/Down to move between months and Shift + Page Up/Down to navigate between years. This ensures users can easily access different periods without using a mouse, adhering to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1. 

Screen Reader Support 

Accessible Labels: The input field should have a clear label, either via <label> or aria-label, to describe its purpose. The current date should be announced when it is selected. The calendar should have aria-live="polite" to announce dynamic updates (such as month changes), adhering to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value. 

Role and State: Use role="combobox" on the input field to signify it has a dropdown, and aria-expanded="true/false" to indicate whether the calendar dropdown is open or closed. In the calendar dropdown, use role="grid" for the calendar grid and aria-selected="true/false" for the currently selected day. This ensures screen readers can interpret the current focus and state of the calendar, in line with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.3: Status Messages. 

Focus Management 

Focus Visibility: Ensure a visible focus indicator on the DatePicker input and on navigable elements within the calendar (such as days, navigation buttons). The focus state should be visually distinct when the user is tabbing through the calendar or input field. This is required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible. 

Logical Focus Order: The focus order should follow a logical sequence when navigating through calendar controls (e.g., from the date input to the calendar dropdown, then to individual days, and finally to navigation controls like the "Today" button or next/previous month). This improves usability for both keyboard and screen reader users, adhering to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.3: Focus Order. 

Error Identification and Handling 

Form Validation: If the DatePicker is part of a form and a valid date is required, use aria-invalid="true" when the input is invalid, and associate an error message with aria-errormessage. For example, if the user fails to select a date, an error message should be announced by the screen reader, following WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3: Error Suggestion. 

Required Field: If the date input is mandatory, use aria-required="true" or the required attribute to notify users that the field must be completed. Ensure that any validation errors are clearly communicated visually and to screen readers, adhering to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.5: Identify Input Purpose. 

Contrast and Visibility 

Text and Calendar Elements: Ensure that all text, including placeholder text, date selections, and calendar controls (days, navigation buttons) have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 for regular text and 3:1 for graphical elements. This ensures users with visual impairments can easily distinguish between different elements in the DatePicker. This adheres to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum) and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast. 

Auto-completion and Input Suggestions 

Autocomplete Behavior: The DatePicker should leverage the browser’s autocomplete functionality where appropriate but should also clearly communicate the expected format to users (e.g., YYYY-MM-DD). Ensure that the user can easily navigate the dropdown options with keyboard controls, in line with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value.

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: 

The input component must be fully operable using the Tab key to navigate between form fields and Enter or Space for submission or interaction. This is essential for keyboard-only users and aligns with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard. 

Ensure that focus is properly managed, especially when an input field opens a dropdown or modal, so that the user can easily return to the form without losing context. 

Screen Reader Support: 

Inputs should always have associated labels. Use the <label> element or aria-label/aria-labelledby for screen readers to identify the input field. This complies with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value. 

Use aria-invalid to communicate input validity. For example, when a field has an invalid input, screen readers will announce that the field is incorrect, adhering to WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification. 

If additional context or explanation is needed for an input (e.g., format or special requirements), use aria-describedby to link the input to supplementary text that explains more, ensuring alignment with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1. 

Focus Indicators: 

Input fields must have visible focus indicators when they are active. This is critical for users navigating via the keyboard, enabling them to see which field is in focus. This guideline follows WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible. 

If the focus changes dynamically (for example, in modal or autocomplete input fields), ensure that the focus management is logical and predictable. This improves the user experience for both keyboard and screen reader users. 

Error Identification and Feedback: 

Form validation errors must be clearly indicated. When an input fails validation, it should trigger both a visual error message and an auditory announcement via aria-errormessage linked to a descriptive element. This ensures that users, including those using screen readers, receive proper feedback, as required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.1: Error Identification and WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3: Error Suggestion. 

If the input is required for form submission, it should be marked with aria-required="true" or the required attribute, and the user should be notified when this requirement is not met. 

Contrast and Visibility: 

Text inside the input field, including placeholder text, must have a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against the background for regular-sized text, as specified by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum). 

Ensure that the input border and any icons or decorations (e.g., validation icons or clear buttons) meet a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 for graphical elements, as required by WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast. 

Auto-completion and Input Suggestions: 

When offering input suggestions (e.g., autocomplete), ensure that the suggestions are easily navigable via the keyboard and that screen readers announce them appropriately. This can be managed by using aria-autocomplete and aria-expanded to signal when options are being displayed, in line with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1. 

Enable users to understand the input’s expected format by providing help text or examples using aria-describedby. 

Form Integration: 

Inputs must be associated with their parent forms using the form attribute or must be embedded directly within the form to ensure proper submission behavior, in line with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.3: Status Messages. 

Ensure the input’s name and value attributes are properly set to capture data during form submission. The name is particularly important to identify the input’s role within the form data. 

Required Fields and Guidance: 

If the input is a required field, it must be clearly communicated to the user, both visually and programmatically (e.g., aria-required="true"). For screen reader users, this ensures they understand which fields must be filled out, in accordance with WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 3.3.3: Error Suggestion. 

Offer guidance text for special input formats (e.g., date, phone number) by linking help text to the input via aria-describedby.

design.content:

Chat Input
Anatomy

Container - The outer frame of the typing line – wraps all the internal components.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When a chat/messaging interface with a system or human representative is required.

When the user is asked to enter free text (question, request, information) instead of choosing from fixed options.

When an ongoing dialogue experience is required – the user sends a message and receives a response.

When it is necessary to offer additional action icons next to the field (send, microphone, file upload).

When to avoid:

When it comes to searching for content on a site/system – there you should use a dedicated search field (Search Input) with a magnifying glass, automatic suggestions and search results.

When there is a clear list of options – it is better to use selection elements (Dropdown, Select, Radio Group) and not allow free text.

When it comes to entering structured information (phone number, date, email) – you should use an appropriate input with validation and not a general text field.

Do's And Don'ts
Do
The submit button should be changed to clickable (default) when you start typing.
Don’t
Don't put a clickable submit button when the search bar is empty.
Do
The input field should be placed at the bottom of the chat.
Don’t
Do not use the chat input field as a regular search.
Examples

Progress bar.name: Progress bar

design.title: Design
design.content:
Anatomy

Track- The complete track that indicates the total length of the process that the Bar Indicator moves over

Bar Indicator- The part that indicates how far the process has progressed out of the complete track

Label- Text that describes the process to which the Progress Bar refers

Help Text- Optional (except in Error or Success mode). Text that helps display additional information about the process taking place. In a state where the progress can be measured (Indeterminate)

He won't show up at all.

Status Icon- Indicates the state of the progress bar, will only appear in Error state or Success state

Progress

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When you want to provide feedback during long operations to inspire confidence in the system's operation among the users, and help them track its progress

To visually display the progress of a system operation such as downloading, uploading, loading data, submitting a form, saving updates, or any other task that has a clear start and end point.

 We will use Indeterminate mode in a long process that can take a considerable or unknown amount of time.

In the other situations we will use when the process can be described using quantitative information, such as a percentage.

When to avoid

When manual user actions are required to progress, it is better to use the Step Indicator.

It should be avoided if the action is immediate that the Progress Bar will turn on and off too quickly to be useful.

To show page loading, for example after filtering data in Dashboard, it is better to use Skeleton.

Highlights:

As soon as the process has finished and reached 100%, the Progress Bar changes to the success mode that appears for one second and moves to the next screen/a loaded image appears.

The minimum width of the Progress Bar is 70 px.

We will not increase the width so that it fills the entire width of the page.

The text in the Label should not change while the Progress Bar is loading. Also, there is no need to update it when the process ends, because information about the success or error is provided by the color of the Bar Indicator or the Status Icon together with the Help Text.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Place the text next to the progress bar
Don’t
Do not insert text into the progress bar




Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: The progress bar should not require keyboard interaction. However, focus should be manageable on the container, especially for users relying on assistive technology.  

Screen Reader Support:  

For Line Progress, provide aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, and aria-valuemax to indicate progress.  

For the Spinner, ensure it has aria-live="polite" to announce its presence to screen readers, as it typically denotes ongoing activity.  

Provide a meaningful label (aria-label) or description (aria-describedby) for both progress types.  

Guidelines:  

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value  

1.3.1: Info and Relationships  

2.4.7: Focus Visible

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:

The appropriate component should be brought according to the size from the Assets panel.

Once the scroll element is inside the outermost frame (which determines the size displayed), the outer frame size of the scroll must be increased
so that it fills the height of the outer frame.

Do's And Don'ts:
Do
Use Scroll when some elements in the list are hidden and visible by scrolling
Don’t
Do not use Scroll when all elements in the list are visible

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

ARIA Roles: Use role="region" or role="complementary" for semantic structure if the scrollable container represents a distinct section of the page. Provide an aria-label or aria-labelledby for context. WCAG 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value  

Keyboard Navigation: Ensure users can tab through interactive elements within the scrollable container. Users should also be able to scroll using the arrow keys, Page Up, Page Down, Home, and End. WCAG 2.1.1: Keyboard  

Focus Visibility: If the scrollable container receives keyboard focus, provide a visible focus indicator. WCAG 2.4.7: Focus Visible

Subtitle

Anatomy

Container - A container that represents the content that will be loaded according to its type (rectangle or circle for images and lines for text)

Types:

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
Highlits:

Skeleton should only be used to produce an entire page loaded for the first time. (If part of the page loads and the bottom part still doesn't load, we'll use a loader). 

Skeleton should be used for pages that load between 2-10 seconds.

When to use:

Use to represent an entire page when loaded.

When to avoid:

Avoid using Skeleton when a specific component within the page has not yet loaded.

Avoid using Skeleton when the top of the page is loaded and the hidden part (below the Fold) has not yet loaded.




Do's And Don'ts:
Do
Use to represent an entire page when loaded.
Don’t
Avoid using Skeleton when a specific component within the page has not yet loaded.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

ARIA Roles: Use aria-hidden="true" to hide the skeleton from assistive technologies since it provides no meaningful content. Ensure the actual content, when loaded, is properly accessible. 

Live Regions: Use aria-busy="true" on the container to indicate to screen readers that the region is loading. Once the content is loaded, set aria-busy="false". WCAG 4.1.3: Status Messages 

Keyboard Navigation: Skeletons should not be focusable, ensuring users navigate only meaningful, loaded content. WCAG 2.1.1: Keyboard

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When you want to provide feedback during long operations to inspire confidence in the system's operation among the users, and help them track its progress

To visually display the progress of a system operation such as downloading, uploading, loading data, submitting a form, saving updates, or any other task that has a clear start and end point.

 We will use Indeterminate mode in a long process that can take a considerable or unknown amount of time.

In the other situations we will use when the process can be described using quantitative information, such as a percentage.

When to avoid

When manual user actions are required to progress, it is better to use the Step Indicator.

It should be avoided if the action is immediate that the Progress Bar will turn on and off too quickly to be useful.

To show page loading, for example after filtering data in Dashboard, it is better to use Skeleton.

Do's And Don'ts
Do
Inside a button, use the small loader
Don’t
Do not use the Progress Bar and Loader together
Do
When loading a screen, use the large loader
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: The progress bar should not require keyboard interaction. However, focus should be manageable on the container, especially for users relying on assistive technology.  

Screen Reader Support:  

For Line Progress, provide aria-valuenow, aria-valuemin, and aria-valuemax to indicate progress.  

For the Spinner, ensure it has aria-live="polite" to announce its presence to screen readers, as it typically denotes ongoing activity.  

Provide a meaningful label (aria-label) or description (aria-describedby) for both progress types.  

Guidelines:  

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value  

1.3.1: Info and Relationships  

2.4.7: Focus Visible

Accordion.name: Accordion

design.title: Design
design.content:
Anatomy

Header- The title bar is clickable, revealing or hiding the content panel.

Arrow Indicator- An arrow that appears at the end of the title. Indicates the state of Expanded (when the content panel is open) or Collapsed (when the content panel is closed).

Icon- A symbol that appears at the beginning of the title - (optional).

Divider- to separate the different titles.

Content Panel- The part that opens when you click on the title. You can insert text into it or insert an additional element using the Slot.

Slot- Used as a placeholder and can be replaced using the Swap Instance with any other component.

Text-Running text that is inside the Content Panel.




States

There are two main states for a component: Collapsed (when the content panel is closed) and Expanded (when the content panel is open).

Each of the modes has the following behaviors:

Mobile:

The component is responsive and can be reduced and enlarged and it will change accordingly.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

To reduce clutter by compressing content into sections that can be explored as needed.

To display a list of items that can be expanded to reveal more detailed information.

Ideal for FAQs (Frequently Asked Questions) where space is limited and the content needs to be organized in a clear hierarchy.

When you need the user to focus on the information displayed on one specific item at a time

When to avoid:

When the content needs to be fully visible and when it is necessary to compare information between different sections.

When a section is too short to hide its accordion part.

It should be avoided for use for main navigation such as a menu, but only the component is used to organize content within the page, it should not be used as a navigation menu.

If all content is equally important, don't hide it in an accordion.

Highlights:

You can click on the entire title bar. By clicking on the title or icon, the content is revealed or hidden and the arrow changes direction.

It is recommended to include up to 6 components.

The number of lines can be increased beyond 6 lines, but it must be taken into account not to create a visual burden on the user.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Use short and clear titles that will make it easier for the user's eyes to review
Don’t
Do not use long titles.
Do
Use the accordion to tidy up the page and shorten scrolling
Don’t
Do not use the accordion for important information that the user may miss.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility
Accordion 

Keyboard Navigation: All headers within the accordion should be focusable via Tab, and users can toggle sections using Enter or Space (WCAG 2.2 Keyboard Interaction). 

Focus Management: Maintain visible focus states and logical focus order across multiple accordion items. 

ARIA Attributes: Use aria-multiselectable="true" when multiexpand is enabled, as well as aria-expanded and aria-hidden attributes on individual accordion items to communicate state to assistive technologies. 

 

Accordion Item 

ARIA Support: Each accordion item should utilize aria-expanded on the header to indicate its current state (open/closed) and aria-controls to tie the header to its associated content. 

Content Visibility: Use aria-hidden="true" for the content of a collapsed panel, ensuring it's hidden from screen readers when not visible. 

Keyboard Accessibility: Ensure each header can be activated by Enter or Space.

Accordion.summary: A vertical list of headers that reveal or hide pieces of content.

Banner.name: Banner

design.title: Design
design.content:
Picture Only

The text is not live text and is part of the image itself. The banner must be designed and inserted as a background image that contains the text (the recommended text size appears on the component)

Live Text Banner- Align to the right

The image is part of the background and the background must be replaced in order to update the image

Live Text Banner- Align to the center

The image is part of the background and the background must be replaced in order to update the image

Anatomy

Container- The container that holds the Banner content

Background Image- An illustration that can be replaced as an image in the element's Fill (variant of the Picture Only, the image also contains the text, recommendations on text size in the element itself)

Title- Concise and prominent text that summarizes the Banner message

Description- Additional details or information to support the title

Footer- Secondary text accompanied by a Link Button linked to another action on the same topic

Action Button- A button that invites the user to perform a certain action related to the banner message

Image with Text- A variant of the Picture Only, the entire banner is an image that contains the text (which is not alive)

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
Guidelines for the Use of Images and Illustrations in the Government Design System:

As part of the government design system, which is intended for the entire population in Israel, it is recommended to choose pictures and illustrations in a way that will suit all sectors, including the ultra-Orthodox and Arab society.
Recommendations for the use of pictures and illustrations: 

- Illustrations are preferred over pictures. 

- If illustrations are used, it is recommended to prefer illustrations of objects and inanimate objects rather than illustrations of people. 

- If you choose to use pictures, it is recommended to avoid images of people (especially women) in order to maintain as wide a cultural accessibility as possible.

These guidelines are not mandatory, but they help create an inclusive, sensitive, and appropriate design for the general public.




When to use:

When it is required to highlight certain content on the screen.

When it is necessary to promote campaigns.

When to Avoid:

Do not use a banner without live text without alt text to avoid accessibility problems

For non-essential information that may confuse the user and distract the user from the main content.

For long content that is more suitable for a dedicated page or section.

Overused, it can be tiring and lead the user to ignore them.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
A large enough space must be kept between the figure and the title in order to leave enough air
Don’t
Do not use more than one banner per page
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

ARIA Roles: Use role="banner" for the main container, aria-labelledby for the title, and aria-describedby for the description to improve screen reader support. 

Keyboard Navigation: Ensure that the action button and footer link are focusable via Tab, and can be activated with Enter or Space. 

Screen Reader Support: Ensure accessible labels are provided for buttons and links, especially for cases where images are decorative. For the main image, use alt text or aria-hidden="true" if the image is decorative.

Banner.summary: The component is designed to convey advertising information or important information that we would like to highlight on the page.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
Guidelines for the Use of Images and Illustrations in the Government Design System:

As part of the government design system, which is intended for the entire population in Israel, it is recommended to choose pictures and illustrations in a way that will suit all sectors, including the ultra-Orthodox and Arab society.
Recommendations for the use of pictures and illustrations: 

- Illustrations are preferred over pictures. 

- If illustrations are used, it is recommended to prefer illustrations of objects and inanimate objects rather than illustrations of people. 

- If you choose to use pictures, it is recommended to avoid images of people (especially women) in order to maintain as wide a cultural accessibility as possible.

These guidelines are not mandatory, but they help create an inclusive, sensitive, and appropriate design for the general public.




When to use:

To present related content or information where the order does not necessarily matter.

To present related content or information where the order does matter.

To present a series of actions or options, search results, or simple data displays.

When to Avoid:

Avoid displaying unrelated items or information to prevent confusion. 

Avoid displaying complex data that requires extensive sorting or interaction. A table would be preferable for this purpose.

Do's & Don'ts
Use an Ordered List if the order of the items in the list is important.
Do
Do not use Unordered List if the order of the items in the list is important.
Don’t
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation  

All list items must be operable via keyboard. Users should be able to navigate between items using the Tab key and activate interactive elements (like more-info buttons) using Enter or Space.  

Ensure focus is placed on more-info content when expanded to prevent focus loss. See WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.1.1: Keyboard.  

Focus Management  

Provide clear, visible focus indicators on interactive elements such as list items and buttons. Focus must follow a logical order. Ensure focus is returned to the toggling button when more-info is closed.  

Relevant WCAG criteria:  

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.3: Focus Order  

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible.  

Screen Reader Support  

Use semantic HTML to ensure proper announcement of list items.  

Ordered and Unordered Lists: Use <ol> and <ul> respectively, allowing screen readers to recognize and announce the number of items.  

Data List (dl) Implementation: Use <dt> for headers and <dd> for descriptive content, making each pair understandable as a name/value relationship.  

Interactive controls (e.g., more-info) should use aria-expanded to indicate their state and aria-controls to associate buttons with their respective content.  

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.3.1: Info and Relationships.  

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value.  

Contrast and Visibility  

Ensure text and non-text elements (like icons) within the list meet the following contrast requirements:  

Text Contrast: Minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text.  

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum).  

Non-text Elements: Minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 for graphical elements like icons and borders.  

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast.  

ARIA Roles and Properties for Data List  

Use role="list" or native <dl>, <ol>, and <ul> tags for appropriate grouping of list items.  

Interactive elements like more-info should use aria-expanded and aria-controls to inform assistive technologies of their state.  

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value.

List.summary: Lists are groups of text or images arranged in a row. Each item in the list can include main actions and extra actions, shown using icons and text.

design.title: Design
design.content:
horizontal
horizontal
vertical
Types

Horizontal / Desktop - Displays updates across the screen

Horizontal / Mobile -  Displays updates across the screen

Vertical - Displays updates across the screen







States

Container - The element that contains the updates.

Text content - Text detailing the update

Date - (Optional) Update date (the newest update will be first).

Update location - Update location (up to 4 updates)

Update navigation - Arrows that allow navigation (in addition to animation of updates)

Divider - Separates update to update and update to date/navigation

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

To display real-time updates such as election results, weather alerts, or news from the field.

To highlight important public messages on relevant pages, such as updates on changes in the availability of government services.

To display emergency alerts immediately and integratively, without disrupting the browsing experience.

As a persistent information element on pages with content such as public portals, government news sites, or real-time information systems.

When to avoid:

When the information is not urgent or time-sensitive – in such cases it is better to use a regular information card or banner.

When it is necessary to display a large amount of text – the component is not suitable for long or detailed content.

In interfaces with high visual load – adding the component may be distracting and burdensome for the user.

When there is a concern that the animation will affect accessibility – for example for users with motion sensitivity.

On pages where the component will be repeated many times – a feeling of congestion and confusion may be created.




Do's and Don'ts
Do
The component must be expanded so that it spans the width of the page (to the margins)
Don’t
The newest update should appear at the top of the list.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content: Accessibility

Updates.summary: The component is used to display short updates, such as emergency updates or public service announcements. The component is positioned to maintain a non-intrusive user experience and updates dynamically.

Breadcrumbs.name: Breadcrumbs

design.title: Design
design.content:
Anatomy

Home- The first page in the route, linking back to the home page or the highest page in the hierarchy.

Current Page- The last page in the route, where the user is now. It cannot be clicked

Page- Any other page in the hierarchy between Home and Current Page

Separator- Used to visually separate the pages

States
Desktop
Mobile

On mobile, we will use one Crumb that serves as a link to the previous page.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When the system has more than two layers in the hierarchy.

When you need to inform the user where he is.

when the user may need to navigate back to a higher level.




When to avoid:

Do not use breadcrumbs on flat-structured sites, or to show progress in a linear journey or transaction.




If there are other navigation elements on the page, such as a sidebar, consider whether users need additional support from breadcrumbs.

Always treat breadcrumbs as secondary and should never completely replace the main navigation. They should not be used for products that have single-level navigation because they create unnecessary clutter.




If you are taking users through a multi-step process, use a progress bar instead.




If a site uses breadcrumbs, they should appear on all pages except the following: the contact page, the home page, the thank you page, the confirmation page (for example, we filled out a form and after submitting we have a successfully submitted page), on login and registration pages, on 404 or error pages.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Use no more than 4 words for a section.
Don’t
Don't use more than 4 words for section. 
Do
Use up to 4 steps
Don’t
Don't display more than 4 steps
Do
If there are more than 4 steps - show the first two and the last two
Don’t
Don't divide the breadcrumbs into 2 rows
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility 

Keyboard Navigation: No special keyboard navigation is needed if breadcrumb links are implemented using native HTML anchor tags (<a>). 

Screen Reader Support: Use aria-label="Breadcrumb" on the <nav> element to provide context and aria-current="page" on the current page link to indicate the active page. Follow these specific WCAG 2.2 guidelines: 

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible: Ensure links have a visible focus state for keyboard users. 

WCAG 2.2 Success Criterion 2.4.7: Focus Visible: Ensure links have a visible focus state for keyboard users.

Breadcrumbs.summary: Breadcrumbs are a navigation element that allows the users to orientate through multiple-hierarchy system that does not contain a Tree. It will always appear right after the header and before the page title.

design.title: Design
design.content:
Navigation Menu
Anatomy

Trigger button- The menu open button.

Menu Container- displays the open state and contains a list of the Container

Menu Item- A single option within the menu.

Icon- (Optional) - An icon that accompanies the Menu Item to provide additional context or indicate the nature of the action.

Submenu Indicator-  Icon indicating that there is a Submenu. Must be used if there is a Submenu.

The Different types of menus:

In all of them you can add an icon and Submenu Indicator, except for the Mobile Header which cannot be changed

Default

Header

Title + Subtitle

States
Mobile behavior

The behavior of the 'Menu Items' is the same as the behavior on the Desktop.

There is a difference in the 'Trigger Button'. The maximum width of the Menu Container will be 5/6 of the screen width.

Closed- The closed state of the Navigation Menu.

Open- The open state of the Navigation Menu where the Trigger Menu becomes a close button.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

Provide navigation options within an interface.

To hide options that are used less frequently. and maintain a clean and focused interface.




When to avoid:

When the options in the interface should be visible and accessible.

If the list has only one or two items, consider using buttons.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
If the Trigger Button is increased beyond 160 px, the menu should also be enlarged according to the same size.
Don’t
The minimum width of the menu is 160 px.
Even if the Trigger Button is smaller than that,
Do not go down from this width.

Tabs.name: Tabs

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When we want to allow content for clear and related categories and sections on the same page.

When users need to quickly move between categories and additional content without leaving the page.

When the content in each tab is of equal importance and should be accessible without excessive scrolling.

When to avoid:

When you need to compare content side by side, since Tabs display one panel at a time.

When the content does not fit logically into separate categories or sections.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Only the neutral Numeric Badge should be used, the meaning of which is clear. It is used for filtering so a user will know how many finds there are.
Don’t
Do not use the red Numeric Badge in Tabs,
Because its meaning wont be clear.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: Use Tab to focus on each tab and Arrow keys to navigate between tabs. Activate a tab with Enter or Space. WCAG 2.2.1: Keyboard Accessibility  

ARIA Roles: Use role="tablist" for the tabs container, role="tab" for each tab, and role="tabpanel" for the tab panel. Use aria-selected on the active tab and aria-controls to associate tabs with their content. WCAG 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value  

Focus Management: Ensure the active tab is announced to screen readers, and focus is visible on keyboard interaction. WCAG 2.4.3: Focus Order

design.title: Design
design.content:
Tabs
Anatomy

Please note: the Container is not an integral part of the component. It is required to build it separately, together with the content
