Toast.name: Toast

design.title: Design
design.content:
Anatomy

Container- The box that contains the message content. Its color describes the status type.

Icon- An icon that describes the status type.

Title- A short text of 2-3 words that precedes the detail. In Floating, you can omit it to reduce space.

Body text- Message details. It is preferable to write one line, maximum two.

Close button- Floating message close button

Link Button- (Optional) A link that redirects to another page.

Border- In inline messages, the outline creates emphasis and separation from the background.

States

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

Should be used for short and simple messages, such as confirmation of an action, a minor error, or quick information.

To display updates that do not require immediate interaction from the user and do not interfere/block the user's continued work.

When to avoid:

When the message is long and complex.

When the message/update is critical, and the interaction with the screen cannot be continued.

When it is required to display a large number of messages/updates simultaneously.

Do's and Don'ts
The user should be told what to do to handle the error.
Do
Do not write error messages without specifying a reason or a recommendation for improvement.
Don’t
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation: Allow keyboard users to close the toast with Tab to reach the close button and Enter or Space to activate it. WCAG 2.2.1: Keyboard Accessibility  

Screen Reader Support: Announce toast messages using aria-live="polite" for non-critical messages and aria-live="assertive" for critical alerts, ensuring timely delivery of content. WCAG 4.1.3: Status Messages  

Color Contrast: Ensure a minimum contrast ratio of 4.5:1 for all text in each variant. WCAG 1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum)

Toast.summary: An update or notification message that integrates with the screen, and does not hide its content.

Tooltip.name: Tooltip

design.title: Design
design.content:
Tooltips

Can be used in Mobile and Desktop

It opens by clicking and closes by clicking on the X icon or anywhere else on the screen.

Intended for a short explanation of up to 42 characters

Anatomy

Container- A box that contains the text and stands out above the background. We will use Inverted mode for graphs only.

Tip- An indicator that links the Container to the UI Trigger (the element that activates the Tooltip). You can choose its direction.

Text - The displayed content.

X icon- The X icon that signifies closing the Tooltip without action when clicked.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

Standard Tooltip

For the sake of describing the action performed using Button.

Popup Tooltip

For the purpose of presenting information that is not critical but that the user may be interested in (see the extension in the government language characterization guide)

When to avoid:

When the information is critical to understanding or operating the interface. This information should be visible and accessible to the user.

When the use will lead to a load on the interface and a negative user experience.

When the information is repetitive and has already been clearly displayed in the user interface.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
Make sure that the tooltip always appears clearly
Don’t
Do not display a cut tooltip.  It should always be whole.
Do
If the information is important, put it in a visible form and not in Tooltip
Don’t
Do not hide important information in Tooltip. Always make sure it is visible to the user.
Do
Use text as short and precise as possible
Don’t
Do not use interactive elements inside a tooltip.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation:  

Focus and Interaction: The tooltip should be triggered via keyboard focus (e.g., Tab key) or by activating the tooltip’s associated element. Once focused, users should close the tooltip using the Esc key, which returns focus to the original triggering element.  

Activation Keys: Tooltips should appear when their associated elements are focused and should disappear on focus out. For users interacting with tooltips through the keyboard, pressing Enter or Space should open the tooltip (if set to click trigger).  

Guidelines:  

2.1.1: Keyboard  

2.4.3: Focus Order  

2.4.7: Focus Visible  

Screen Reader Support:  

ARIA Roles and Properties:  

Use role="tooltip" to denote the tooltip content, allowing screen readers to announce it appropriately.  

Associate tooltips with triggering elements via aria-describedby. This ensures the tooltip content is announced when the focus lands on the triggering element.  

The optional close button inside the tooltip should be focusable, with aria-label="Close tooltip" for clarity.  

Live Region Announcements: For tooltips that appear automatically, use aria-live="polite" to announce dynamic updates without interrupting the user.  

Guidelines:  

1.3.1: Info and Relationships  

4.1.2: Name, Role, Value  

Focus Management:  

Tooltips should be visible when the associated element is in focus and should not disrupt the focus order. If the tooltip is dismissed (e.g., by clicking the close button), the focus should return to the triggering element.  

Ensure the tooltip's close button (if present) has a clear, visible focus indicator.  

Guidelines:  

2.4.7: Focus Visible  

2.4.3: Focus Order  

Contrast and Visibility:  

Text Contrast: Ensure the tooltip text has a contrast ratio of at least 4.5:1 against the background for readability, particularly with dark themes.  

Non-Text Contrast: Visual indicators like close buttons, borders, and background colors should meet a minimum contrast ratio of 3:1 to ensure accessibility for users with low vision or color blindness.  

Guidelines:  

1.4.3: Contrast (Minimum)  

1.4.11: Non-text Contrast

Tooltip.summary: A floating, non-actionable label used to explain a user interface element or feature.

Modal.name: Modal

design.title: Design
design.content:
Anatomy

Overlay- A semi-transparent background that covers the entire screen to focus attention on the Modal.

Container- The container that contains the content.

Title- The modal title

Content Area- The main body of the modal, where text, forms or other interactive elements are displayed.

Scroller- Indicates that the text is scrollable

Action Button- One or more buttons that allow the user to perform a task or cancel the modal.

Types

There are 4 types for the component:

For the first three types, we will add a layer of Overlay in the Overlay/default color behind

Simple Modal

Long Text Modal

Modal with Slots- Allows to integrate interactive components in Modal (such as Input Field, Radio Button...)

Coach Mark Modal

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
Guidelines for the Use of Images and Illustrations in the Government Design System:

As part of the government design system, which is intended for the entire population in Israel, it is recommended to choose pictures and illustrations in a way that will suit all sectors, including the ultra-Orthodox and Arab society.
Recommendations for the use of pictures and illustrations: 

- Illustrations are preferred over pictures. 

- If illustrations are used, it is recommended to prefer illustrations of objects and inanimate objects rather than illustrations of people. 

- If you choose to use pictures, it is recommended to avoid images of people (especially women) in order to maintain as wide a cultural accessibility as possible.

These guidelines are not mandatory, but they help create an inclusive, sensitive, and appropriate design for the general public.




When to use:

When it is required to show the user critical information that requires immediate action by the user, however, the use of the component should not be overdone because it is intrusive.

When it is required to collect information from the user without leaving the current page.

When you want to display step-by-step processes in the wizard without leaving the current page.

When to avoid:

To display large amounts of content, consider creating a separate page.

When the information or action is not critical enough to interfere with the user's workflow.

If the content may confuse or cause a disruptive experience.

Do and Don'ts
Do
Add an additional layer in Overlay/default color behind all modal types (except Coach Mark Modal)
Don’t
Do not use more than 5 lines of text in Simple Modal. For this we will use the Long Text Modal that comes with a Scroller for scrolling the text.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

ARIA Roles: Use role="dialog" on the modal container. Attach aria-labelledby to the title and aria-describedby to the description for screen reader context. This ensures that users understand the purpose and content of the modal. WCAG 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value 

Keyboard Navigation: Focus should be trapped within the modal when it is open. Users can navigate interactive elements (e.g., close button, action buttons) with the Tab key, and pressing Escape should close the modal. WCAG 2.1.1: Keyboard and WCAG 2.4.7: Focus Visible 

Focus Management: When the modal opens, set focus to the first interactive element (typically the close button). On close, return focus to the element that triggered the modal, preserving user context. WCAG 2.4.3: Focus Order 

Screen Reader Support: Use aria-modal="true" to prevent screen readers from interacting with content outside the modal. Ensure that the close button and action buttons are labeled clearly, using aria-label for accessible button descriptions. WCAG 2.4.6: Headings and Labels 

Live Announcements: If the modal contains dynamically updated content (e.g., status messages or error notifications), use aria-live to announce changes without interrupting the user’s interaction with the modal. WCAG 4.1.3: Status Messages

Modal.summary: The component makes it possible to focus the user's attention solely on the task or information, without losing the context of the current page. The component requires user action in order to close it.

Drawer.name: Drawer

design.title: Design
design.content: Anatomy

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When we want to reduce clutter by hiding content that is not essential to the main workflow but is still accessible when needed

When there is limited screen space and a navigation bar might take up too much space

When to avoid:

Avoid if the content is critical to the main workflow and should be visible at all times.

 Make sure the component does not disrupt the user experience such as hiding important information or controls.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
A 16 px margin must be maintained on all sides.
Don’t
Do not shorten the drawer height below the screen height.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

ARIA Roles: Use role="dialog" for the Drawer container to indicate a modal interaction. Include aria-labelledby for the title or heading and aria-describedby for additional content description. WCAG 4.1.2: Name, Role, Value  

Keyboard Navigation: Trap focus within the Drawer while it is open. Allow closing via Escape key and ensure the close button is accessible via Tab. WCAG 2.1.1: Keyboard  

Focus Management: When the Drawer opens, set focus to the first focusable element (e.g., close button). When it closes, return focus to the element that triggered it. WCAG 2.4.3: Focus Order  

Overlay Management: Prevent interaction with background content while the Drawer is open using aria-hidden on other elements or focus trapping. WCAG 1.4.11: Non-text Contrast

Drawer.summary: A panel that extends from the edge of the screen and serves as a place for additional navigation or options without creating a clutter on the main display.

Tour Guide - Spotlight.name: Tour Guide - Spotlight

design.title: Design
design.content:
Spotlight
.Spotlight Content
.Spotlight Content
Anatomy

Elemant Highlight - The emphasis is on the UI element for which the explanation is given.

Spotlight - A box that displays instructions/explanation of the highlighted element and is adjacent to it. 

Pointer (Tip) - A visual pointer (arrow) aimed at the highlighted element.

Title (Optional) - A short title summarizing the purpose of the stage.

Description - Text that explains the element or provides instructions for action.

Actiom Buttons - Control buttons such as "Next", "Previous", "Skip" or "Close", which allow you to navigate the process

Stage Counter - A step counter (e.g. "1/3") that shows the user's position in the manual and helps track progress.

Media - Used to display, image, or a short animation that supports the message visually.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

To guide new users and guide them through key components of the interface, during the first visit.

To present new features or significant changes, while emphasizing and explaining them.

For guidance in complex tasks, where the action is not intuitive or involves multiple steps.

When to avoid:

When the explanations are simple. Tooltip is basic enough, even in a new interface.

When used frequently. Repeated use can tire the user and be perceived as annoying.

During important or time-sensitive processes (such as payment or submitting a form).

When the elements cannot be focused – you should avoid emphasizing elements that cannot be highlighted or interacted with.

Highlights
Spotlighted Element

A 4px-thick frame should be added around the highlighted element, in a color called a spotlighted element and a Level-1 shadow. The frame is designed to make it easier to identify the element to which the Spotlight is referring, and to strengthen the connection between the prompt and the content on the screen.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
The Spotlight should be placed next to the relevant element, so that there is a direct and clear connection between them.
Don’t
Don't place the Spotlight far from the element it's displaying.
Do
The Spotlight should be placed next to the relevant element, taking care not to hide other important elements.
Don’t
Don't place the Spotlight in a way that hides important elements of the screen.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content: Accessibility

Tour Guide - Walkthrough - Modal.name: Tour Guide - Walkthrough - Modal

design.title: Design
design.content:
Walkthrough - Modal
Walkthrough - Modal
Walkthrough - Modal
Walkthrough - Modal
Anatomy

Background Overlay - A layer that darkens the rest of the interface. Focuses attention, and prevents interaction with the interface.

Modal Container - A centered dialog box, containing the tutorial content.

Media - Used to display an image or short animation that visually supports a message.

Title - A concise title that presents the purpose of the stage or its main message

Description - Text that explains the element or provides instructions for action.

Action Bottons - Control buttons such as "Next", "Previous", "Skip" or "Close", which allow navigation through the process.

Stage Counter - A step counter that shows the user's position in the guide and helps track progress.

Close Button - Allows the dialogue to be closed at any point in the process.




Types

Moltiple Step's - A tutorial experience that guides the user through a number of actions or functions. It is recommended to limit the number of steps to 3–4 at most.

Single Announcement - A one-time message explaining a new feature or change in the system, without navigation steps.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

To clearly demonstrate the value of a product and its core functionality.

To guide users through an initial setup process (such as creating an account or setting preferences).

To explain new features or significant changes after a product update.

To assist users in completing complex or multi-step tasks.

To bring returning users back into the picture by showing what’s new since their last visit.

When to avoid:

Do not use too frequently or for small changes and minor updates.

When users are in the middle of a critical task,

As a substitute for a good user experience – do not rely on training to explain unintuitive flows or design issues.




Highlights
Overlay Layer

An overlay layer should be placed that covers the entire screen, in order to focus the user's attention on the modal content and prevent interaction with the interface behind it.




Do's and Don'ts
Do
The Walkthrough – Modal should be placed in the center of the screen, above the Overlay layer,
Don’t
Do not place the Walkthrough – Modal on the sides of the screen,
Do
The Walkthrough - Modal should be placed above the Overlay layer, so that it is the only prominent element on the screen and focuses the user's attention.
Don’t
Do not place any additional elements other than the Walkthrough – Modal above the Overlay layer,
Examples

accessibility.content: Accessibility

Error Message.name: Error Message

design.title: Design
design.content:
Error message
Error message
Anatomy

Error Message - A clear message indicating the problem, for example: "Page not found."

Supporting Text - A brief explanation of why the user is seeing the message, for example: "The page may have been removed or never existed."

Navigation Option - A button that guides the user to relevant areas of the site (e.g., the home page).

Illustration - A visual element that reinforces the message and improves the user experience. (The element that takes the place of the illustration can be replaced with the appropriate illustration via the swap instance).

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

404 Error: When a page or URL no longer exists or was entered incorrectly.

Removed or moved pages: When pages previously located in a specific location on the site have been removed or moved to a new location

Blocked or unauthorized page access attempt: In the case of accessing a page that the user is not authorized to view.

When to avoid:

Technical issues not related to a specific page: If there are general technical issues on the site (such as network connection or server errors), avoid displaying the "Error message" element and use a generic error message.

Other error messages: If it is an error that can be resolved immediately (such as a form not being completed correctly), do not use the "Error message" element, but rather a customized message that provides an immediate solution.

Do's and Don'ts
Do
The error message must be worded in accordance with the government language specification guide, for example: using simple, non-high-level language
Don’t
Do not write error messages that do not explain what the problem actually is (it is not enough to write "error").
Don’t
Do not use exclamation marks.
Examples

Error Message.summary: A message that is automatically generated by the system and informs the user of an unwanted situation. The component presents the user with a clear and accessible error message and offers navigation back to relevant areas of the site to improve the user experience.

design.title: Design
design.content:
Table Raw Dark
Table Raw Light
Table Raw Long Text Dark
Table Raw Long Text Light
Header
Slot
Anatomy

Column Header - A single header cell associated with a single column.

Tooltip Icon - (Optional) icon that opens the Tooltip. Suitable for non-critical information that users may be looking for. You need to create a tooltip with the additional explanation. 

Sorting Icon - An icon that you click on arranges the data in the same column in ascending or descending order.

States
Column Header Cell Item
Raw Cell Item

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
How to use
How to use sticky cells







When to use:

When we want to present data that is best understood when presented in relation to other data.

To display comparative analysis – when users need to compare values between different categories or variables.

Dashboard-reporting when users need to analyze and interpret complex information.

In administrative interfaces—when users need to manage content, settings, or data entry that requires a detailed and structured layout.

When to avoid:

When the data can be displayed more effectively in a list or in another simpler format.

On mobile – if the table contains too many columns to fit comfortably on a small screen, consider using a different element or design template.

Narrative content – when the information is best presented in the form of a paragraph or as part of the flow of a story.

For data that requires visualization – where a representation such as a chart or graph will be more effective in communicating the data.

Do

Don’t

Don’t

Filter- Horizontal.name: Filter- Horizontal

design.title: Design
design.content:
Anatomy

Container- Fixed width that contains all the elements for filtering.

Dropdown- Maximum of 5 units, with the option to reduce the quantity so that they fill the width of the container.

Checkbox- Maximum of 5 units, with the option to choose the quantity through the Properties

Apply button- Clicking on it applies the selected filters to the dataset. You can choose whether or not it is needed depending on the development.

Clear button- Clicking it clears all selected filters and resets the display to its original state.

*** The component is fixed on the screen and does not open or close.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When you want to filter extensive lists or information - Large Dataset

When you want to narrow down search results, and help find the most relevant results

Data tables - allow you to display only the rows that meet certain criteria

To customize the display of metrics or reports based on specific parameters in the Dashboard

When to avoid:

Avoid when the full list can be seen without further filtering and using filtering would add unnecessary complexity

When too many filters can lead to a lack of results (over-filtering)

If filtering data could cause the user to miss critical information

In real-time, constantly changing data, filters can become outdated quickly

When there is a high probability that the user will need to select a single option, consider using a different component, for example: Switch

Do's and Don'ts
Do
If you want to show less than 5 Dropdowns, you must manually delete up to the desired number and the remaining Dropdowns will fill the width of the Container. Using a Filter with two rows, if you want to reduce the number of Dropdowns, we will use the Dropdown in Empty mode (in order to maintain a uniform width of the Dropdown).
Don’t
Do not open the dropdown within the filter itself. For development, the open state should be shown on the side.
Examples

accessibility.title: Accessibility
accessibility.content:
Accessibility

Keyboard Navigation 

Tab/Shift+Tab: Navigate between filter fields and action buttons. 

Arrow Keys: Navigate within dropdown and checkbox options. 

Enter/Space: 

Open/close dropdowns.

design.title: Design
design.content:
Bottom navigation - Mobile
Bottom navigation - Mobile
Anatomy

Label – Text that describes the page the link navigates to. 

Icon – An icon that accompanies the text to provide additional context 

Chosen Indicator Line – A line indicating that the option is selected 

Bot Badge – A small, round element without text, indicating that there is a new update or change in status. 

Numeric Badge – A small round element that displays one or more digits, indicating the number of items requiring attention. 




States

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When there are between 3 and 5 main destinations of the application (sections), each of which is equally important. 

When each destination represents a first navigation level (top-level destination). 

When the user is expected to navigate frequently between the destinations. 

When the use is mainly on mobile – the component is adjusted to the height of the thumb and allows comfortable navigation with one hand. 

When you want to give high visibility to each of the destinations without hiding them in an additional menu (like a hamburger menu) 

When to avoid:

When there are more than 5 main goals – this will overload the interface, reduce the clickable areas and harm usability. 

When the goals are not at the main level but are considered part of deeper content – ​​in such cases it is better to use in-page navigation or other menus. 

When the application requires one main central action (such as taking a photo, writing, recording), and it needs to be given priority – in such cases a FAB (floating action button) can be more suitable. 

When there is already a fixed top navigation bar, and Bottom Navigation would burden the user interface or conflict with existing design principles. 

When the main navigation changes between screens – Bottom Navigation is intended for a consistent navigation structure throughout the application 




Guidelines for using the Top and Bottom navigation bar

When and how to use Top Navigation (top bar) and Bottom Navigation (bottom bar) in mobile applications (iOS and Android):

Top Navigation Bar

Appears at the top of the screen.

Contains: title, back button, icons for actions (such as search, settings).

Used for internal navigation and the context of the current screen.

Bottom Navigation Bar

Appears at the bottom of the screen.

Contains: icons with text for navigation between main areas of the app (for example: home, search, profile).

Used for primary navigation between top-level screens.

When do we use both?

When there are several main areas in the application (for example: Home, Messages, Profile).

When each area also requires unique actions (like a filter/edit button).

Example: Instagram, YouTube - there is a bottom navigation bar and a top bar for actions on the screen.

When do we use only one?

Only a top bar - when:

 The application is linear/hierarchical. 

There is no need to navigate between fixed main areas.

Example: Document or settings application.

Only a bottom bar - when:

A minimalist design is desired.

The actions within each screen are simple or not required.

Example: TikTok (screens without a title at the top).







Do's and Don'ts
Do
Only 3 to 5 goals should be presented, with an icon and clear text for each one.
Don’t
Do not allow scrolling in the bottom menu.
Do
You should use the Badge to alert about new or important information.
Don’t
Do not use to split content (for that there are tabs)
Do
Navigation options should be consistent across all screens (so that on each screen the relevant option is the one that is 'selected')
Don’t
Do not use icons without text only - it hampers understanding, especially for new users.
Do
99+ should be written when there is a three-digit number (or more)
Don’t
Do not write a long number on the badge.
Examples

Bottom Navigation.summary: A fixed navigation element located at the bottom of the screen, providing quick access to the main sections of a mobile application. The element helps users navigate between main screens easily, while maintaining context for the current screen.

Highlights and differences in the use of the top navigation bar on Android and iOS.
Back Button

iOS

Arrow left, sometimes including the name of the previous screen.

Automatically appears if there is hierarchical navigation.

Android

Arrow left or hamburger menu

The control is in the hands of the designer - can decide whether to show or not

There is a "Back" button as part of the Android system.




Actions - Icon Buttons

iOS

Icons appear only on the left side (in English - on the right side), usually one or two.

Generally, there is no menu.

Android

Support for a menu on the left side that can contain several actions.

There is more flexibility in adding icons.




Scrolling and Sticky Top Navigation Bar

Sticky Top Navigation

When the top navigation bar is set to be sticky and remains attached to the top of the screen during scrolling – a subtle shadow should be added to it. The shadow clarifies to the user that the bar is 'floating' above the scrolling content, and helps to distinguish the boundary between the bar and the content.

Scrolling Top Navigation

When the navigation bar is not sticky, but scrolls together with the content - there is no need for a shadow, as there is no need to create a distinction between the bar and the content beneath it.

usage.title: Usage
usage.content:
When to use:

When there is a hierarchy of screens - the top navigation will provide a back button and an appropriate title for each level 

When it is necessary to display the screen title - to make it clear to the user where they are 

When there are important actions related to the current screen 

When there is no bottom navigation component (Bottom Navigation) 

When building a dedicated mobile application (iOS/Android) with a need for a fixed title and navigation. 

In forms or multi-step processes. 

When to avoid:

On responsive websites or interfaces – a Web-compatible header should be used 

in situations where the top navigation does not add significant information 

when navigation is done only through gestures (e.g. a full-screen photo gallery). 

when system navigation elements already exist (such as a header or system buttons).

Used for primary navigation between top-level screens.

When there are several main areas in the application (for example: Home, Messages, Profile).

When each area also requires unique actions (like a filter/edit button).

Example: Instagram, YouTube - there is a bottom navigation bar and a top bar for actions on the screen.

When do we use only one?

Only a top bar - when:

 The application is linear/hierarchical. 

There is no need to navigate between fixed main areas.

Example: Document or settings application.

Only a bottom bar - when:

A minimalist design is desired.

The actions within each screen are simple or not required.

Example: TikTok (screens without a title at the top).







Do's and Don'ts
Do
A long title should be displayed in the large component - intended for that.
Don’t
Do not display a very long title in the component when it is small.
Do
The back button should be used in internal screens in the hierarchy.
Don’t
Do not display a back button on the home screen or if there is nowhere to go back to.
Do
Scrolling of content below the bar should be allowed without it disappearing unless that is your intention (Scroll behavior)
Don’t
The bar should not be hidden unless it is a very specific case (like watching in full screen).

The component allows users to understand their location in the application structure, navigate back through hierarchical navigation screens, and perform actions relevant to the active screen.

How do you start working with the governmental design system? All the details here.

UX/UI Design

The government design system has a ready-made component library in the Figma design tool. 

To install the library and quickly and easily pull components into your interfaces, follow these simple steps:

Obtain a Figma License: You can easily order Figma licenses through the Yehalom system. For large organizations, we recommend choosing an Enterprise license, which allows for project management in teams according to the organization's team divisions. Please note: Without a paid license, you cannot use the full capabilities of the system.




Install the Israeli Government Design System Library: First, open the government design system file from the Figma Community. Second, define the file as a Library: In the top menu, click "Publish" to publish the library. And that's it! You have quick access to all components in all organization files, via the Assets tab.

Please Note: Avoid detaching components. If there is a shortage, contact the design system team to complete the shortages comprehensively for all design system users and to maintain consistency.

Contact Racheli at Rachelik@digital.gov.il

When publishing version updates to the government design system, download the design system file from the Figma website again and reinstall it as a library.

Want to stay updated? Join our WhatsApp group: https://did.li/TqPTY
